etch.title: Micro Etching Test
intro: A micro etching test shows the internal structure of the metal. A sample is cut from the material or the finished part, polished to a mirror finish and treated with an etching solution that reveals the grains and grain boundaries. The etched surface is then examined under a microscope.

We carry out micro etching tests in-house on the stainless steel, carbon steel and nickel alloy material used for our anchors, studs and fabricated parts. The test shows whether forming, welding or heat treatment has left the material in the condition the specification requires.

tests.title: Intergranular attack screening
tests.text: An electrolytic oxalic acid etch that screens austenitic stainless steels, such as 304, 310, 316 and 321, for sensitization: chromium carbides at the grain boundaries that make the material prone to intergranular corrosion. It is used to check material after welding or heat treatment, and to confirm that solution annealing has dissolved the carbides.

tests.title: Microstructure and grain size
tests.text: Microetching to ASTM E407 reveals the microstructure of stainless steel, carbon steel and nickel alloys. The average grain size is then rated to ASTM E112, and the structure is checked for excessive grain growth and unwanted phases.

tests.title: Weld macro etch
tests.text: A welded stud or anchor is cut through the weld, polished and etched so that the fusion zone becomes visible. The section shows whether the weld has fused across the full stud base and how far it has penetrated into the base metal. EN ISO 14555 uses this macro examination to qualify stud welding procedures.

etch.readingTitle: How ASTM A262 Practice A results are read

reading.title: Step structure
reading.text: Steps between the grains and no ditches at the grain boundaries. Acceptable: the material is not sensitized.

reading.title: Dual structure
reading.text: Some ditches at the grain boundaries, but no grain completely surrounded by them. Acceptable.

reading.title: Ditch structure
reading.text: One or more grains completely surrounded by ditches. The material is classed as suspect and must pass the hot acid test that ASTM A262 specifies for the grade (Practice B, C or E) before it can be accepted.

etch.readingNote: Practice A is a screening test: it can accept material but cannot reject it. It applies to austenitic stainless steels only, so nickel alloys and carbon steel are checked for microstructure and grain size instead.
etch.productsText: The test applies to our metal products, especially stainless steel parts that are cold formed, welded or heat treated before delivery. Insulation materials such as mineral wool, ceramic gaskets and calcium silicate are not metallic, so micro etching does not apply to them.
etch.requestText: The micro etching report can be supplied with the other test certificates for your order. Name the test and the standard in your enquiry.

bsaPage.metaTitle: Bright Solution Annealing for Refractory Anchors | Santura Engineering
bsaPage.metaDescription: Vacuum bright solution annealing for stainless steel and nickel alloy refractory anchors. Since 1980, exporting to 25+ countries. ISO 9001:2015.
bsaPage.h1: Bright Solution Annealing for Refractory Anchors
bsaPage.subheading: Vacuum heat treatment that restores atomic equilibrium in cold-worked stainless steel and nickel alloy anchors and extends their service life.
what: Solution annealing heats stainless steel or a nickel alloy above its solution temperature, typically between 1040 °C and 1230 °C depending on the alloy, holds it long enough for the structure to recrystallise, and then cools it rapidly. This dissolves carbides and other precipitates and returns the metal to its original, fully austenitic microstructure.
In bright solution annealing the work is heated in a vacuum or under an inert gas such as argon. No oxygen reaches the surface, so the anchors come out clean and bright, with no oxide scale.

Conventional "black" annealing in air darkens the surface and forms oxide scale. The scale must be removed afterwards, and the metal lost to it reduces the effective cross-section of the anchor, which matters on thin wire and strip.
bsaPage.whyTitle: Why it matters for refractory anchors
bsaPage.whyIntro: Making an anchor involves cold drawing, bending, forming and welding. Each step distorts the crystal lattice and leaves internal stresses stored in the metal as dislocations. Left untreated, these stresses make the anchor vulnerable in three ways.

risks.title: Corrosion
risks.text: Cold-worked, highly stressed metal is more susceptible to stress corrosion cracking and to attack by the sulphur, chlorides and alkalis found in furnaces, kilns and boilers.

risks.title: Sigma phase embrittlement
risks.text: At service temperatures of roughly 600–900 °C, cold-worked stainless steel forms sigma phase faster. This hard, brittle phase sharply reduces toughness, so the anchor can crack once the unit cools down.

risks.title: Shorter service life
risks.text: Stressed anchors lose strength and fail earlier under repeated heating and cooling, often before the refractory lining itself is due for replacement.

whyResult: Bright solution annealing releases these stresses and returns the atoms to their equilibrium spacing, the condition in which the alloy performs best at high temperature. It also dissolves any carbides or sigma phase already present.
The result is an anchor that resists corrosion and embrittlement for longer and keeps its mechanical strength at service temperature.

bsaPage.tableNote: Each alloy needs its own temperature and soaking time; incorrect parameters can damage the material instead of improving it. Santura's process follows ASTM A240 and the applicable material specification for each grade.

faq.q: What is the difference between bright and black solution annealing?
faq.a: Bright annealing is carried out in a vacuum or inert gas, so the surface stays clean and free of oxide. Black annealing is carried out in air, which forms oxide scale that must be removed and reduces the effective cross-section of the anchor.

faq.q: Which alloys can be bright solution annealed?
faq.a: All the austenitic stainless steels used for refractory anchors (304, 309, 310, 316 and 321), the heat-resistant grade 253MA, and the nickel alloys 800H, 601 and 625.

faq.q: How do you verify that BSA was done correctly?
faq.a: By hardness and tensile testing. Treated material should be softer than untreated material, with hardness back in the annealed range for the grade and tensile strength close to the specified minimum. The surface should also be bright and free of scale. A micro etching test to ASTM A262 Practice A, carried out in-house, confirms that the chromium carbides have been dissolved.

faq.q: Does BSA increase anchor service life?
faq.a: Yes. By removing the internal stresses left by cold working and restoring atomic equilibrium, BSA-treated anchors resist corrosion and sigma phase embrittlement significantly better than untreated anchors.

ppPage.metaTitle: Pickling & Passivation for Refractory Anchors | ASTM A380 A967 | Santura Engineering
ppPage.metaDescription: Pickling and passivation of stainless steel refractory anchors per ASTM A380 and A967. Since 1980, exporting to 25+ countries. ISO 9001:2015.
ppPage.h1: Pickling & Passivation for Stainless Steel Refractory Anchors
ppPage.subheading: Acid cleaning and surface treatment that remove weld scale, heat tint and embedded contaminants, restoring full corrosion resistance before installation.
ppPage.whatIntro: They are two distinct processes. When both are specified, pickling comes first and passivation follows.

pickling.title: Pickling
points: An aggressive acid treatment, usually with a mixture of nitric and hydrofluoric acids.
Removes weld scale, heat tint, oxide layers, embedded iron particles and other contamination left by welding, cutting, grinding and bending.
Dissolves a thin layer of the surface itself, exposing fresh base metal underneath.
Leaves a uniform matte finish, free of discoloration and contaminants.
Applied by tank immersion for complete parts, by spray for large fabrications or site work, or as a brush-on gel for welds and small areas.

passivation.title: Passivation
points: A milder acid treatment, using nitric or citric acid.
Does not remove metal; it removes free iron and other surface contaminants only.
Helps the natural chromium-oxide passive layer, which gives stainless steel its corrosion resistance, to form.
The passive layer forms in air on its own, but on freshly fabricated surfaces that process can be impaired. Passivation makes sure it forms completely and uniformly.
After pickling, passivation rebuilds the protective layer on the clean surface. It can also be specified on its own for parts that need no descaling.

ppPage.whyTitle: Why it matters for refractory anchors
ppPage.whyIntro: Anchors are cut, ground, bent into V and Y shapes, and welded to furnace shells and ductwork. Each step damages the surface in a different way.

damage.title: Weld heat tint
damage.text: The coloured oxide around a weld forms by drawing chromium out of the metal just beneath it. The passive layer cannot form properly in that chromium-depleted zone.

damage.title: Grinding
damage.text: Grinding wheels and carbon steel tools leave embedded iron particles that rust and start corrosion on an otherwise stainless surface.

damage.title: Cutting
damage.text: Cut edges are rough and stressed, and corrosion starts there first.

whyResult: Left untreated, these damaged areas are the first points of failure in high-temperature service, and the chromium-depleted zones around welds are the most vulnerable of all.

Pickling removes the damaged layer entirely, and passivation rebuilds the chromium-oxide film on the clean surface. The result is an anchor with uniform corrosion resistance over its whole surface, including welds and bends.

standards.a380: Standard Practice for Cleaning, Descaling and Passivation of Stainless Steel Parts, Equipment and Systems. Covers the cleaning and pickling process.
standards.a967: Standard Specification for Chemical Passivation Treatments for Stainless Steel Parts. Covers passivation treatments and how to verify them.
standards.verify: Copper sulfate test, which confirms that the surface is free of iron contamination and properly passivated.

materials.title: Austenitic stainless steels
materials.text: SS304, SS304L, SS309, SS310, SS310S, SS316, SS316L, SS321 and SS347.

methods.title: Tank immersion
methods.text: The whole batch of anchors is immersed in the acid tank. Best for high volumes of small and medium parts.

methods.title: Spray pickling
methods.text: Acid is sprayed onto larger fabricated assemblies. Suitable for site work and oversized components.

methods.title: Brush-on gel
methods.text: Pickling paste applied to specific welds or spots. Used for field repairs and targeted treatment of heat-affected zones.

ppPage.methodsNote: Parts must be degreased and cleaned of oil, grease and other organic contamination before acid treatment. Pickling and passivation do not remove oil or grease.
ppPage.whenTitle: When to specify pickling and passivation
when: After welding anchors to furnace shells or ductwork.
After heat treatment: pickling removes the scale left by solution annealing in air, and bright-annealed parts can be passivated where specified.
When anchors show visible heat tint or weld discoloration.
When anchors have been in contact with carbon steel tools during fabrication.
For critical service in refineries and petrochemical plants, and for stainless fabrications for the pharmaceutical and food industries.
When the end customer’s specification calls for ASTM A380 or A967 compliance.

faq.q: What is the difference between pickling and passivation?
faq.a: Pickling is an aggressive acid treatment that removes weld scale, heat tint and a thin layer of metal. Passivation is a milder acid treatment that removes free iron and helps the protective chromium-oxide layer re-form. They are usually done in sequence.

faq.q: Why do refractory anchors need pickling and passivation?
faq.a: Welding, bending and cutting damage the surface and deplete chromium in the heat-affected zone. Without treatment, these areas are the first to corrode in high-temperature service.

faq.q: What standards apply to pickling and passivation?
faq.a: ASTM A380 covers cleaning and pickling. ASTM A967 covers passivation treatments and their verification; the copper sulfate test (Practice D) confirms that the surface is properly passivated.

faq.q: Can pickling and passivation be done on site?
faq.a: Yes. Spray pickling and brush-on gel allow welded assemblies and large fabrications to be treated on site.

pmiPage.pmiLinkFromQuality: More about our PMI testing service
what: Positive material identification (PMI) is a non-destructive test that measures the elemental composition of a metal and confirms its alloy grade. It is carried out with a portable X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analyser or an optical emission spectrometer (OES).
The analyser reads the composition in seconds and matches it against a library of alloy grades. Nothing is cut, drilled or damaged, so finished anchors can be tested and shipped.
pmiPage.whyTitle: Why it matters for refractory anchors

why.title: The wrong alloy fails in service
why.text: An anchor in SS304 where SS310 was specified can oxidise, lose strength and fail at furnace temperature, taking the refractory lining with it.

why.title: Mix-ups happen
why.text: Material can be mixed up in production, storage or shipping. Labels can be wrong and mill certificates can be matched to the wrong batch.

why.title: The final check before dispatch
why.text: PMI is the last verification that every anchor leaving the factory is the alloy the customer ordered.

why.title: Required by end users
why.text: Refineries and petrochemical plants often apply material verification programmes based on API RP 578 and ask for PMI reports before accepting materials on site.

methods.title: Portable XRF
methods.text: Handheld X-ray fluorescence gives a reading in seconds, anywhere in the works. It is the standard method for checking raw material, work in progress and finished anchors.

methods.title: OES (optical emission spectroscopy)
methods.text: Spark OES also measures carbon and light elements. It is slower, less portable and leaves a small burn mark, so it is used when carbon content must be confirmed.

methods.title: Laboratory analysis
methods.text: Where a specification calls for full chemical analysis, samples are tested at NABL-accredited third-party laboratories.

pmiPage.limitationText: XRF does not detect carbon, so it cannot tell SS316 from SS316L, or SS304 from SS304L. When low-carbon grades must be confirmed, OES or laboratory analysis is used.

faq.a: The alloying elements that identify a grade, including chromium, nickel, molybdenum, titanium, niobium and manganese, and silicon on suitable analysers. The analyser matches the measured composition to an alloy grade.

swPage.h1: Stud Welding Solutions for Refractory Anchors
swPage.subheading: Anchors, stud welding equipment, ceramic ferrules and welding procedures for fast, reliable installation on furnace and vessel shells.
what: Stud welding fixes a refractory anchor directly to a furnace or vessel shell with an electric arc, in a fraction of a second and without drilling holes.

The stud welding gun holds the anchor against the shell and strikes an arc that melts the end of the stud and a small zone of the shell. The gun then plunges the stud into the molten pool, which solidifies into a full-section weld.
In drawn arc welding a ceramic ferrule surrounds the weld, containing the molten metal and shielding it from the air.

compareRows.da: Tenths of a second to about 1 second

compareRows.label: Ceramic ferrule
compareRows.sc: No; gas shielding can be used for stainless steel

swPage.whyTitle: Why weld quality matters in refractory service

why.title: The weld holds the lining
why.text: Anchors are welded to carbon steel or stainless steel shells before the lining is installed. Every kilogram of refractory hangs on those welds.

why.title: A poor weld fails first

why.title: The right process for each anchor
why.text: Castable anchors with stud bases need drawn arc welding, ceramic fibre studs and insulation pins need capacitor discharge, and some anchors are designed for manual welding or bolting.

why.title: Shutdowns leave no time for rework

faq.q: What is the difference between drawn arc and capacitor discharge stud welding?
faq.a: Drawn arc welding uses a longer arc and a ceramic ferrule to weld larger studs, up to about 25 mm, to shells from about 2 mm thick, giving deep penetration and high strength. Capacitor discharge welds smaller studs, up to about 10 mm, in a few milliseconds without a ferrule, and suits thin material down to about 0.7 mm.

faq.q: Which method is used for which anchor type?
faq.a: Castable anchors with stud or gun-weldable bases, such as SEPL-06, SEPL-13 and SEPL-18, use drawn arc welding. Ceramic fibre studs (SEPL-24), weld-on threaded studs (SEPL-25) and insulation pins use capacitor discharge. Some anchors, such as SEPL-07 and SEPL-09, are designed for manual welding.

faq.q: Can anchors be supplied ready for welding on site?
faq.a: Yes. Anchors are supplied with stud bases or pre-welded studs prepared for site installation, together with matching ferrules and recommended welding parameters.

faq.q: Which ceramic ferrule sizes are available?
faq.a: Ferrules are matched to the stud diameter and to the surface being welded, such as flat plate or tube. Tell us the stud diameter and shell geometry and we will supply the matching ferrules with the anchors.

faq.q: How is stud weld quality checked?
faq.a: By macro etching. A test stud is cut through the weld, polished and etched in-house, which shows whether the weld has fused across the full stud base and how far it has penetrated into the base metal. For stainless steel anchors, a micro etching test to ASTM A262 Practice A also checks the material for sensitization.

swPage.etchText: Weld quality is checked by macro etching. A test stud is cut through the weld, polished and etched in-house, so that the fusion zone and the depth of penetration can be examined. This is the macro examination that EN ISO 14555 uses to qualify stud welding procedures.

odPage.overviewTitle: What observation and peep doors do
overview: Observation doors and peep doors are access panels built into the walls of furnaces, boilers, kilns and heaters. They let operators look inside the vessel, check the flame, inspect the refractory lining and insert thermocouples or probes, all without opening the vessel or stopping the process.

Each door has a steel frame that is bolted or welded to the vessel shell, a door or cover that closes the opening, and a refractory lining that matches the lining of the wall around it. Anchors welded inside the frame hold that lining in place, the same way refractory anchors hold the lining of the vessel wall.

Santura fabricates observation doors in-house in its fabrication shop, in stainless steel or hot-dip galvanized mild steel, with refractory anchors, hardened glass and gaskets fitted to the customer's specification.

overview: Foundation bolts are steel bolts embedded in a concrete foundation to hold down structures, columns, equipment and machinery. The embedded end is bent, hooked or fitted with a plate so it cannot pull out of the concrete; the threaded end projects above the foundation to take the baseplate, nut and washer.

The terms are often used for the same product. Anchor bolt usually describes a bolt cast into concrete, while foundation bolt describes a bolt that secures equipment to its base. Many foundation bolts are fitted with a pipe sleeve around the upper part, which leaves room to adjust the bolt position slightly when the equipment is set.

Santura makes foundation bolts as part of its custom fabrication work: bar is cut, bent, threaded and hot-dip galvanized to the customer's drawing. We make headed, bent and threaded foundation bolts in diameters up to 6 inch and above.

faq.q: What is the difference between L-type and J-type foundation bolts?
faq.a: Both have a bent embedded end. An L-type bolt is bent at 90 degrees, while a J-type bolt has a curved hook. The L-type is the most common choice for columns and baseplates; the J-type is used for lighter connections such as pipe supports and handrails, and can give better pull-out resistance in some layouts.

faq.q: What is ASTM F1554?
faq.a: ASTM F1554 is the American standard for anchor rods that are cast into concrete. It covers straight, bent and headed rods in three grades, 36, 55 and 105, named after their minimum yield strength in ksi. The projecting end is colour coded: blue for Grade 36, yellow for Grade 55 and red for Grade 105.

faq.q: Can you make foundation bolts in custom lengths?
faq.a: Yes. We cut, bend and thread every bolt to the customer's drawing, from about 150 mm to 3000 mm and longer. The thread length, bend length and bend radius are made as specified.

faq.q: What finishes are available for foundation bolts?
faq.a: Hot-dip galvanizing to ASTM F2329 is the most common finish for outdoor and embedded bolts. Zinc plating (yellow, blue or white) suits indoor and mild environments, black oxide gives basic protection, and bolts can be supplied plain when specified or when made in stainless steel.

faq.q: What are refractory support plates?
faq.a: Refractory support plates, also called lining support brackets or consoles, are steel brackets welded to the inside of a furnace or boiler shell. They carry the weight of the refractory lining, especially in tall vertical walls and overhead sections, and spread that load evenly across the shell. They are also used to support burner blocks separately from the wall.

faq.q: What materials are support plates made from?
faq.a: Structural plates are usually mild steel to IS 2062 or ASTM A36, or ASTM A572 Grade 50 for heavy loads. Boiler and pressure vessel parts use IS 2002 or SA 516 Gr 70. Refractory support brackets that run hot are made in stainless steel such as SS304 or SS310, and SS316 is used in corrosive environments.

faq.q: Can plates be supplied machined?
faq.a: Yes. Base plates can be machined flat on the bearing face for full contact with the grout, and holes are CNC or manually drilled to the drawing tolerance. Plates can also be supplied shot blasted, primer painted or hot-dip galvanized.

faq.q: What is the maximum plate thickness available?
faq.a: We supply support plates from 6 mm up to 100 mm thick and above, cut to drawing from plates up to 2000 × 6000 mm. Thick plates can be ultrasonically tested where the specification requires it.

faq.q: What is a ball type stanchion?
faq.a: A ball type stanchion is a handrail post with forged steel balls fixed along its length. The horizontal rails pass through holes in the balls and are locked in place with grub screws. This makes the handrail quick to assemble and lets rails meet the post at the angle needed for stairs and corners.

faq.q: What handrail height does OSHA require?
faq.a: OSHA 1910.29 requires the top edge of the top rail to be 42 inches (1067 mm) above the walking surface, plus or minus 3 inches. A mid rail is needed where there is no wall or parapet, toe boards must be at least 3.5 inches (89 mm) high, and the top rail must withstand a force of 200 lb (890 N).

faq.q: What is the difference between a single and a double ball stanchion?
faq.a: A single ball stanchion carries only a top rail. A double ball stanchion carries a top rail and a knee rail halfway down, which is the standard arrangement for most industrial platforms and walkways because the knee rail closes the gap below the top rail.

faq.q: Can stanchions be supplied galvanized?
faq.a: Yes. Hot-dip galvanizing after fabrication is our standard finish for mild steel stanchions used outdoors and in industrial plants. Stanchions can also be supplied powder coated, in primer for painting on site, or in stainless steel with no coating.

pgPage.overviewTitle: What pipe guides and ring sleeves are
overview: Pipe guides and ring sleeves are fabricated steel parts that support, guide and protect piping and furnace tubes. A pipe guide stops a pipe moving sideways while still letting it grow and shrink along its length as the temperature changes.

A ring sleeve, also called a pipe sleeve or penetration sleeve, is a cylinder fitted where a pipe passes through a wall, floor or vessel shell. It protects the pipe, seals the opening and leaves room for the pipe to move.

Both matter most in fired heaters, boilers and furnaces, where piping runs hot and goes through repeated heating and cooling. Santura makes pipe guides and ring sleeves to the customer's drawing, including parts for heaters built to API 560.

faq.q: What is a pipe guide used for?
faq.a: A pipe guide keeps a pipe on its line. It stops the pipe moving sideways but lets it slide along its length as it expands when hot and contracts when it cools. Guides are placed along long pipe runs and near expansion joints and loops so that thermal movement goes where the designer intended.

faq.q: What is API 560?
faq.a: API 560 is the American Petroleum Institute standard for fired heaters used in refineries and petrochemical plants. It covers design, materials, fabrication and testing, including the tube supports and guides inside the firebox. For example, it limits the unsupported horizontal tube length to 35 tube diameters or 6 m, whichever is less.

faq.q: What is the difference between a pipe guide and a pipe support?
faq.a: A pipe support carries the weight of the pipe. A pipe guide controls the direction it can move: it stops sideways movement while allowing lengthwise expansion. Many guides also carry weight, so a guide is a support that also restrains the pipe in one or more directions.

faq.q: What is a ring sleeve?

cwPage.subheading: Lever-arm counter-weight systems that carry the weight of radiant tubes in hydrogen reformers and ethylene cracking furnaces. Made by Santura since the late 1990s, to the client's engineering drawings.
cwPage.photoAlt: Galvanized counter-weight lever arm assembly with dead weight stacks
cwPage.photoCaption: Galvanized lever arm assembly with dead weight stacks at our workshop.
what: In hydrogen reformers and ethylene cracking furnaces, vertical tubes hang inside the firebox at very high temperatures. Reformer tubes are filled with catalyst, and each tube with its catalyst can weigh more than a tonne. The tubes grow noticeably longer as they heat up.

A counter-weight system carries this weight so the tube can hang freely and expand and contract without stress. It works on the lever principle: a dead weight on one end of a pivoted lever arm balances the tube on the other end.
The pivots must move with almost no friction. Even small friction forces would push unwanted load into the tubes, which shortens their life.
how: Hanger rods run from the top of each tube, up through the furnace roof, to a yoke.
The yoke connects to one end of a horizontal lever arm, which pivots on a fulcrum frame on the roof structure.
A calculated dead weight hangs from the other end of the lever arm.
The dead weight balances the catalyst-filled tube, the lower pigtail, its share of the floating manifold, half the upper pigtail and the suspension hardware.
As the tube heats up and grows downwards, the lever arm tilts slightly and the dead weight rises, so the support force on the tube stays constant.

faq.q: What is a counter-weight system in a reformer?
faq.a: It is a lever system on the furnace roof that carries the weight of each reformer tube. A hanger rod connects the tube to one end of a pivoted lever arm, and a calculated dead weight on the other end balances it. When the tube heats up and grows, the lever tilts and the support force stays the same, so the tube can expand without stress.

faq.q: Why are Graphalloy bushings used?
faq.a: Graphalloy is a graphite and metal composite bearing material that runs without oil or grease and keeps working at high temperatures. Every pivot in a counter-weight system must move with almost no friction, because friction would push extra load into the tubes. Lubricated bearings dry out or seize in this service, so oil-less Graphalloy bushings are used instead.

faq.q: What material are the pivot pins?
faq.a: Our pivot pins are special grade stainless steel 410S, a martensitic stainless steel with good corrosion and heat resistance. They run in stainless steel clevises machined at our Mumbai workshop.

faq.q: What is the difference between rockwool and glass wool insulation?
faq.a: Rockwool (stone wool) is made from basalt rock, handles temperatures up to 750 °C and has a higher density (30–200 kg/m³), which makes it the choice for high-temperature industrial insulation. faq.q: What temperature can mineral wool insulation withstand?

faq.q: What thicknesses and densities are available?

faq.q: Is mineral wool insulation safe and asbestos-free?

overview: Calcium silicate is a high-temperature, lightweight, abuse-resistant and asbestos-free industrial insulation. It is made of hydrous calcium silicate with reinforcing fibres and formed into rigid shapes: slabs, preformed pipe sections, bevelled lags and powder. It keeps its insulating properties even after wetting and drying.

It fills the gap between soft mineral wool and ceramic fibre. Unlike soft insulation, it is rigid and self-supporting, so it withstands foot traffic and knocks on pipe racks and equipment, while keeping low thermal conductivity, high compressive strength and very little shrinkage over its service life.

faq.q: What temperature can calcium silicate insulation withstand?
faq.a: Calcium silicate insulation is rated for continuous service up to 1000–1100 °C, depending on the grade. It keeps its structure, low thermal conductivity and compressive strength across its rated range, and retains its insulating properties even after wetting and drying.

faq.q: What forms of calcium silicate insulation are available?
faq.a: Calcium silicate is available as rigid flat slabs and boards, preformed pipe sections (half-shells), bevelled lags for large pipes, curved segments for vessels and columns, and powder for cavity fill. Standard pipe sections fit inside diameters from 15 mm to 600 mm in thicknesses from 25 to 100 mm. Other sizes are made to drawing.

faq.q: What standards does your calcium silicate conform to?
faq.a: Our calcium silicate conforms to ASTM C-533, IS 8154 (flat blocks), IS 9428 (pipe sections) and BS 3958 Part II. It is non-combustible with zero flame spread in ASTM E-84 surface burning tests, asbestos-free and free of VOCs.

faq.q: What are the advantages of calcium silicate over mineral wool insulation?
faq.a: Calcium silicate works at higher temperatures (up to 1100 °C, against 750 °C for rockwool), is much stronger and more abuse-resistant, is rigid and self-supporting so it withstands foot traffic and impact, and performs consistently after wet-dry cycles. Mineral wool is more flexible and costs less below 750 °C. We supply both.
